Quash

KWOSH -- from Old French quasser, from Latin quassare ('to shake, shatter'); a genuine cousin of squash. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To quash to reject or void something officially and completely, or to forcefully put an end to something.

City hall moved swiftly to quash speculation that the beloved community pool would be demolished for a parking garage.

Worked Example

The union quickly moved to quash reports that a wildcat strike was being planned, worried the rumor alone could derail contract negotiations.

The union didn't just ignore the rumor -- it acted decisively to stop and invalidate it completely, which is what it means to quash something.

How Quash Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

nullify

nullify: to make something legally void or without effect

suppress

suppress: to forcibly put an end to something

Antonyms

uphold

uphold: to confirm or support something, such as a decision

ratify

ratify: to formally approve or confirm something

How Strong Is It? — nullify → quash → suppress

nullify vs. quash

nullify vs. quash: A single typo was enough to nullify the entire contract.

suppress vs. quash

suppress vs. quash: The government moved swiftly to suppress the uprising before news of it could spread.

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Quash traces back to Latin quassare, 'to shake or shatter,' by way of Old French quasser -- to quash a ruling or rumor is to shatter it completely.

Use the root in a new word: squash

Use the root in a new word: squash: The verb squash (to crush flat) comes from that very same Latin root, quassare, by way of Old French -- quash and squash are true etymological cousins.

Word Choice

Quash is a fairly formal word, common in legal contexts (quashing a subpoena or indictment) but also used more broadly for shutting down a rumor, rebellion, or plan before it can gain momentum.
